transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... honestly, my wife really pushed for it, and my director at work kind of heavily suggested it, in a way. The thing is, I just can’t seem to stop launching projects. And I know, I'm an IT manager, so planning and executing is literally my job, I've got my degree in it, it's what I do. But lately this is... it's different. It's like a switch gets flipped and I just start initiating everything all at once. 

I’m drafting these massive, sweeping work plans for the department that go way beyond my actual scope, and at the exact same time, I’m drawing up these intense, minute-by-minute study schedules for myself to knock out multiple advanced certifications in a fraction of the time it normally takes. But it doesn't stop at the office, you know? I get home and I immediately start tearing into the drywall for these huge home network upgrades—running new cable, configuring new hardware, setting up a whole new server rack. And while I'm doing all of that, I'm constantly firing off messages to old contacts, vendors, people I haven't talked to since college, just trying to get all these different initiatives off the ground. 

It just gets so incredibly intense. It's like this motor running inside me that I can't shut off, and I just completely blow past normal limits. I don't even realize how far over the line I am until my wife has to literally step in and take the crimping tool out of my hands, or my director actually has to pull me into a closed-door meeting to intervene and tell me I need to hit the brakes. So... yeah, that's why I'm sitting here. They think I need to get it checked out.
Do you feel unusually happy or euphoric when you're launching all these projects?

Well, happy is... I mean, yes and no, it’s complicated. It’s more like... electric, you know? Unstoppable. Like my brain is firing on all cylinders and I’m seeing the connections between everything—the servers, the certifications, the departmental workflow—and it all just makes perfect sense. I get this rush, this absolute surge of energy where I feel like I could conquer the world, or at least rebuild our entire IT infrastructure in a weekend. And during those weeks, I feel fantastic, honestly. I feel like I’m finally operating at my true potential. 

But then... the flip side of that is, well, it doesn't take much to completely derail that feeling. If I'm in the zone, pulling Cat6 cable through the living room wall at 2 AM, and my wife comes out and asks me to keep the noise down, or if a vendor takes more than an hour to reply to an email about a bulk hardware order... I just snap. It’s like this blinding flash of frustration. I get so intensely irritated, because to me, it feels like they’re intentionally throwing up roadblocks. Like everyone around me is moving in slow motion and they’re actively trying to drag me down to their speed. I know logically my wife just wants to sleep, but in the moment, it feels like she’s sabotaging my progress. So it's not just pure happiness... it’s this high-voltage energy that turns into pure rage the second someone gets in my way.
Do you ever find yourself feeling really down or depressed?

Yeah... yeah, I do. And it's... it's such a jarring contrast, you know? Because when I'm up, I'm so up, but then... there are these stretches. It's like the power just cuts out. The servers crash, the network goes dark, and I'm just left sitting in the quiet. 

When it hits, I wake up and I just feel... heavy. Flat. Like all that electricity is just gone, drained out of me completely. I lie there in bed and I just feel like this absolute, failed version of myself. I look at the holes in the drywall, the half-finished server rack, the fifty emails I started drafting to vendors, and instead of feeling that drive to finish it all, I just feel this crushing weight of... I don't know, inadequacy? Like, who do I think I am, trying to do all of this? I'm just a fraud. I'm a failure. 

And getting out of bed during those times... it feels like I'm moving through wet concrete. The simplest things become monumental tasks. Even just... my wife, she'll ask me something totally normal, like what I want for dinner or if I paid the water bill, and it just feels like too much. It's overwhelming. I can't even process the question, let alone formulate an answer. I just want to pull the covers over my head and disappear. It's not just a bad day, it's this deep, sinking feeling that everything I do is pointless, and that I'm completely useless. And it can last for weeks, just this slow, agonizing slog through the days where I can barely function, let alone manage a whole IT department. It's... it's really hard to explain just how empty it feels compared to the high.
Do your low or depressed periods usually happen after one of these intense, energetic periods?

Well, you know, you'd think so, right? Like, what goes up must come down, that kind of logic. You'd think the crash would always just naturally follow the... the surge, the manic energy, or whatever you want to call it. And sometimes it does, sure. Sometimes I burn the candle at both ends, running cables and drafting proposals until I literally just collapse into this heavy, dark place. But... no, it's not actually that predictable. It's not a neat little sequence of events. 

Sometimes the darkness just creeps in out of nowhere, completely unprovoked. I could be having a totally normal week—no massive projects, no staying up till 3 AM configuring routers, just doing my regular 9-to-5, coming home, eating dinner with my wife... and then, boom. I wake up one morning and it's like someone pulled the plug on the server. Just dead. And other times, I'll have one of those intense, high-voltage weeks where I'm redesigning the entire office network architecture, and when it finally wraps up, I don't crash at all. I just kind of... level out. Go back to baseline. 

So, no, there isn't really a strict pattern to it, which honestly makes it so much harder to deal with. If I knew that every time I went overboard with a project I was going to pay for it with a month of depression, maybe I could try to manage it better, or at least brace myself for the impact, you know? But because it's so random... it's like living with a faulty motherboard. You never know when it's going to short out, or why. I've spent hours trying to chart it out—literally, I built a spreadsheet trying to correlate my project initiation dates with my low moods, tracking sleep hours, caffeine intake, even the weather, trying to find some kind of algorithm to explain it. But the data just doesn't line up. It's totally erratic.
Do you feel like you're back to normal between these intense, energetic periods?

Well, normal is... I mean, what is normal, really? But if you mean, do I go back to feeling like my regular self, not supercharged and not dragging through the mud... yes, I do have those periods. There are definitely times, sometimes stretching out for a few weeks at a time, where my energy is just... stable. Calm. Flat, even, but in a good way. I'm not staying up all night re-wiring the house, and I'm not stuck in bed unable to face the day. I'm just going to work, doing my job, coming home. 

But... and this is the part that really messes with my head, doctor... even during those quiet weeks, when my mood is totally fine, the other stuff doesn't always go away. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk, feeling completely even-keeled, but I'll look at the Microsoft Teams statuses of my staff, and I'll still see the patterns. I'll still know, deep down, that when Dave goes from 'Available' to 'Away' at exactly 10:14 AM, and then Sarah sets hers to 'Do Not Disturb' two minutes later... it's a coded warning. It's a signal they're sending about me, about my job security or some audit they're planning behind my back. I know it sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but in the moment, even when I'm not manic, it feels like an absolute fact. 

And the voices, too. Not full conversations, usually, but just... brief comments. I'll be in the server room, completely alone, just doing routine maintenance, feeling totally fine, and I'll hear someone say my name, or mutter something like, "He missed a spot," or "Watch him." Just quick, little jabs. And I'll spin around, and there's absolutely no one there. The security badge reader hasn't beeped, the door is locked... it's just me and the hum of the cooling units. So, yeah, my mood might be perfectly normal, but my brain is still... processing things that aren't there. It's like the operating system is running fine, but there's this background process I can't kill that keeps throwing up these bizarre error messages. It's exhausting, honestly, because I can never fully let my guard down, even when I'm supposed to be at baseline.
Do you ever believe things that aren't true, even when there's evidence to the contrary?

Well, "not true" is... I mean, it’s a tricky concept, isn't it? Because in the moment, it feels like the absolute, undeniable truth. But... yes. Yes, I suppose so. Because my logical brain—the IT manager brain, the guy who deals in binary and server logs and hard data—knows that there’s evidence against what I'm thinking. My wife will point it out, or I'll even point it out to myself, but it just doesn't matter. The belief just completely overrides the facts. 

Like I was saying a minute ago about those quiet weeks, where my mood is totally fine and I’m not in a big swing either way... the paranoia, or whatever you want to call it, it just doesn't shut off. It’s the Teams statuses, sure, but it goes so much deeper than that. It’s calendar invites, too. I’ll get a totally standard Outlook invite from my director for a "Q3 Alignment Sync" or a "Quick Touchbase," and my stomach just drops. I can look at my recent performance reviews—they’re stellar, I literally got a bonus last quarter, there is physical, financial evidence that I am doing a good job—but I will look at that calendar invite and become absolutely convinced that it's a coded warning. 

And it’s not just digital, it’s in the office, too. I’ll walk past the breakroom to get coffee, and I’ll hear two of the junior devs talking in low voices, and maybe one of them says something completely innocuous like, "We need to pivot on this strategy." But my brain just locks onto it. Pivot. They’re pivoting away from me. I'll get back to my desk and I am just consumed by this absolute certainty that these hallway comments, the calendar invites, the status changes... they are all connected. I get convinced that they are actively building a case to push me out of the company. 

I’ll sit there for hours, completely ignoring my actual work, just combing through my sent folder, trying to find the exact email they’re going to use as ammunition to terminate me. I’ll map out who was in the breakroom, what time the invite was sent, trying to reverse-engineer their plot. And the crazy thing is, part of me knows I'm doing it. Part of me is screaming, "Look at your bonus check! Look at your track record! No one is firing you!" But that logical voice is just a whisper compared to this overwhelming, crushing belief that the axe is about to fall. It just... it takes over everything, even when I have all the proof in the world that I'm safe.
Do you ever see things that aren't there?

See things? No, no, I don't think I've ever really seen anything that wasn't there. My vision is fine, I'm not seeing people standing in the corner of the room or shadows moving or anything cinematic like that. It's not a visual thing for me. But... well, like I was saying a few minutes ago about the server room, it's the sounds. It's hearing things. That's the part that really gets me, and it's just so incredibly distracting.

It’s almost always embedded in the background noise. Like, you know how a server room sounds, right? Or maybe you don't, but it's this constant, heavy hum. We've got these massive HVAC units keeping the server racks cool, plus all the high-RPM fans on the hardware spinning at once. It's just a solid wall of white noise. And it's right in the middle of that hum—or even when I'm working from my home office and the house is totally dead quiet except for my PC fan—that's when I hear it. 

I'll just be sitting there, maybe running a routine diagnostic or updating a database, and clear as day, I'll hear my name. Just my name, spoken right behind my ear. Or it'll be these short, clipped little comments. Someone muttering, "check the logs," or... or "they know." 

"They know." That one really, really gets under my skin, especially with everything else I was telling you about the Teams statuses and the calendar invites. I'll be sitting in my home office—I have this setup in the spare bedroom, I even added some soundproofing panels so I wouldn't wake my wife when I'm on late-night calls with the overseas devs—and I know for an absolute, verifiable fact that I am the only person awake in the house. My wife is asleep, the doors are deadbolted. But I'll hear "they know" coming from just over my left shoulder. 

And I'll completely freeze. I'll pull my headset off, I'll check the security cameras on my phone, I'll even walk out into the hallway... nothing. Nobody is there. But the voice sounds so real, so perfectly real, that I'll spend the next three hours completely derailed. I'll literally log into the VPN and start checking the firewall logs because the voice told me to "check the logs," and I'll be tearing my hair out trying to figure out who "they" are and what they "know." So, no, I don't see things, but what I hear... it’s so vivid it completely hijacks my reality anyway.
How long do your low or depressed periods usually last?

Well, time is... time gets a little distorted with this stuff, to be perfectly honest. But because I'm an IT guy, I like data, right? I like to have metrics and hard facts to look at. So I've actually tried to quantify this. I've gone back through my Outlook calendar, my PTO requests, even my commit history on our repositories just to see when I was actually productive and when I was just... a ghost. 

Because when those low periods hit, it's like a complete system failure. I go from being hyper-vigilant, checking all those server logs and Teams statuses like I was telling you about, to just... nothing. The bottom just falls out. I withdraw completely. I won't talk to my wife, I'll just sit in the dark in my home office, ignoring the blinking lights on the router and the monitors, feeling completely empty and heavy. I can barely drag myself to the keyboard to send a one-line email, let alone manage a team of developers. It's like my brain is running in safe mode, just barely executing the absolute minimum background tasks to keep me breathing.

And I was trying to figure out exactly how much of my life this has eaten up. Because it comes and goes, right? Sometimes it's a couple of weeks here, maybe a month or so there where I just can't function properly and I'm dragging myself through the mud. But if you take all of that, if you aggregate the data over this whole course of whatever is happening to me... all those low, withdrawn periods have added up to about seven months. 

Seven months. It's terrifying when you actually put a number on it like that. Seven months of my life just being completely offline, emotionally and physically. And the hardest part is that when I'm in it, it feels like it's never going to end. I just sit there thinking about how much time I'm losing, how my team is probably having to pick up my slack, which, of course, just feeds right back into the paranoia later when my energy comes back and I start thinking they're building a case to fire me for being unproductive. It's this vicious cycle, doctor, and it just feeds on itself. But yeah, cumulatively, if you look at the whole timeline... it's been about seven months of just being totally withdrawn and shut down.
Have you ever lost a job, damaged a relationship, or gotten into legal trouble as a direct result of your intense, energetic periods?

Legal trouble? No, no, thankfully I've managed to avoid anything with the police or the courts. But... the job and the relationships? Yeah. Yeah, it’s definitely taken a toll. 

I mean, I haven't been outright fired, but I was actually put on mandatory administrative leave recently. It was right after this massive database migration we were doing. When I get into one of those really intense, high-energy gears, I feel like I can process a million threads at once, right? Like my brain is just completely overclocked and I don't need sleep, I don't need breaks. So I basically took the entire migration on myself. I was up for days, completely bypassing our standard QA protocols because I was just so utterly convinced I had optimized the deployment pipeline perfectly and that everyone else would just slow me down. But I was moving too fast. I missed a critical dependency, and the whole migration completely failed. It took down our primary client portal for hours. My director had to put me on leave to "recenter," which... well, it was humiliating. Especially with how paranoid I get about my job security anyway. 

And at home, it's... it's really hard on my wife. She basically has to step in and act like an emergency brake when I get like that. Because the late-night work just spirals totally out of control. I’ll be in the home office at 3 AM ordering thousands of dollars of enterprise-grade networking equipment on our joint credit card because I suddenly decide I need to build a proprietary local cloud environment in the spare room. She literally has to physically come in, take the credit card away, and try to talk me down from the ledge regarding the spending. 

And when she does that, or when she just tries to get me to shut the monitors off and come to bed... I get so irritable. My thoughts are moving so fast that I feel like she's just dragging me down, and these simple, everyday conversations turn into these explosive, exhausting arguments. I just talk over her, pace around the house, getting defensive... it’s not fair to her. She shouldn't have to manage me like a rogue employee.

And it bleeds into everything else, too. I used to have a life outside of work, you know? I was playing bass for the music team at our church, I was really into indoor rock climbing, and I even did this weekend mentoring program for high school kids interested in coding. But I’ve pulled away from all of it. Every single bit of it. Because I just can’t reliably show up anymore. If I’m in one of those intense periods, I’ll commit to a dozen extra volunteer shifts and then completely blow them off because I got obsessed with a new coding project, or I’ll show up to climbing and just be totally reckless and talk everyone's ear off until they're uncomfortable. And then, of course, the crash comes, and I can't even get out of bed. I just can't follow through on anything consistently, so I just... I had to drop it all. It’s just easier to isolate than to keep letting people down.
Do you think your high-energy periods and low, depressed periods are connected, or do they feel like separate things to you?

That is a really good question, actually, and man, I wish I knew the answer. I really do. Because if I knew how they were connected, or if I could prove that they were, maybe I could actually predict them, right? 

Like I was saying before, I'm a data guy. I look for patterns. In any normal enterprise network environment, if server A suddenly spikes to 100% CPU usage and then server B completely crashes two hours later, you immediately look for the dependency. You assume there's a connection, a causal link, and you dig into the logs to find it. So I've tried to look at my own brain, my own life, exactly like that. I've literally sat down with this massive whiteboard I have in my home office—the one I bought when we first transitioned to remote work, it takes up almost half the wall—and I've tried to chart out the timeline of my moods, just trying to find some kind of verifiable metric. 

But honestly? I just don't know. I can't figure it out at all. Sometimes, it really does feel like the crash is a direct result of the high-energy phase. Like my brain just completely runs out of RAM, overheats, and does a hard, ungraceful reset. Like after that database migration failure I was just telling you about, where I was up for days? I crashed so incredibly hard right after that. Just completely flatlined. So when that happens, you'd think, okay, there it is, cause and effect. What goes up must come down, they are definitely connected. 

But then... there are all these other times where the data doesn't support that at all. I'll just be humming along, totally normal baseline, just doing my daily stand-ups, managing my team's Jira tickets, having dinner with my wife, and out of absolutely nowhere, the floor just drops out. I'll plunge right into one of those dead, heavy periods for weeks, and there was absolutely no high-energy phase beforehand. No warning, no manic late-night coding sessions, nothing. Just a sudden system failure out of nowhere. Or, conversely, I'll have a period where I'm totally wired, pacing the house, talking a mile a minute, and then it just kind of... fizzles out. It just fades back into a normal week without any crash at all. 

So, are they connected? Are they just two completely different, unrelated bugs in my system? I have absolutely no idea. It's incredibly frustrating, doctor, because my entire career is based on being able to troubleshoot complex systems, to find the root cause of an issue and patch it. I'm the guy people call when they can't figure out what's wrong. But with this, with my own head, I'm just flying totally blind. I keep trying to analyze the variables—I've looked at my sleep logs, my diet, my stress levels during different project sprints—but the data just doesn't line up cleanly. It's just a mess. So, yeah, I really don't know what to make of it. I'm at a total loss.
Do you ever hear voices or experience other unusual perceptions when you're feeling really down or depressed?

Voices? When I'm... when I'm in the crash? No. No, actually, it’s almost exactly the opposite of that, if I'm being perfectly honest. When I'm really down, when the system just completely halts like I was describing earlier... there's no extra input at all. If anything, it's like a total loss of signal. I'm not getting false audio artifacts or, you know, hearing people talking to me when nobody's in the room. It’s just... dead air. 

You know when you put on a pair of high-end noise-canceling headphones, but you haven't started playing any music yet? And there's just that heavy, almost pressurized silence that kind of rings in your ears because it's just so profoundly empty? That’s exactly what the low periods feel like to me. I'll be sitting there in my home office, the monitors are asleep, the house is perfectly quiet, and I'm just drowning in that silence. 

I mean, I hear my own thoughts, obviously. But it's very clearly *my* voice, just my own internal monologue running this endless, exhausting loop of how I'm letting my wife down, how I'm dropping the ball on the current sprint at work, how I'm basically a defective unit. But it's definitely me thinking it. It’s not some external voice or some, you know, separate entity broadcasting into my head. 

And I don't see things either, not when I'm depressed. The room might feel physically heavier, or the shadows might seem a bit deeper because I haven't opened the blinds in three days and I'm just sitting in the dark, but there are no visual anomalies. No ghosts in the machine, so to speak. Honestly, in a weird, twisted way, I almost wish there was something like that to analyze? Because at least a voice or a vision is a data point. It's an active error code you can log and track. But the depression is just... a void. It's a complete lack of data. Just me and the absolute, crushing quiet. So, to answer your question, no. No voices, no unusual perceptions when I'm down. Just a whole lot of nothing.
Have you ever experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt abnormally happy or euphoric, had increased energy, and were more active than usual?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. Two weeks is definitely a solid benchmark for it, sometimes it even stretches a bit longer, maybe three or four weeks if I'm really in the zone. Abnormally happy is one way to put it, but "euphoric" really hits the nail on the head. 

It's like... you know when you upgrade a network from legacy copper wiring to pure fiber optic? Suddenly the throughput is just infinite, there's zero latency, and everything is just flowing perfectly. That's exactly how my brain feels. Some weeks I feel almost electric and unstoppable. I'll wake up at 4 AM and I don't even need coffee, I just sit down at my rig and I'm instantly compiling code in my head, mapping out architectural diagrams, feeling like I can solve every single problem our company has ever had before lunch. It's an incredible high. I feel like a superhero, honestly. Like I'm operating on a completely different, higher frequency than the rest of the world, and I'm just churning out these massive, visionary ideas. 

But... and this is where it gets really tricky, and where it ties back into what I was saying earlier about my wife having to manage me... that electric feeling has a very, very sharp edge to it. Because when I'm moving at a million miles an hour, the rest of the world is still moving at dial-up speeds. And my patience for that is absolutely zero. 

So if I hit a tiny delay—like, a server takes three extra seconds to ping back, or a junior dev submits a pull request with a basic formatting error, or even just... just my wife walking into the home office to ask me a totally normal, simple question like what I want to do for dinner... I just snap. I mean, I go from this euphoric high to just pure, unfiltered rage in a millisecond. I'll snap at her, or I'll snap at my team, because in my head, it feels like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose. It literally feels like they are deliberately throwing wrenches into the gears just to sabotage my momentum when I am clearly on the verge of a massive breakthrough. 

I'll yell, I'll pace around the room, I'll get incredibly defensive... it's like my tolerance for anything less than instant execution is just completely gone. So it's this incredibly intense mix, right? I'm on top of the world, I'm euphoric, I have boundless energy, I'm getting a month's worth of work done in a single weekend, but the second someone interrupts that flow, I turn into an absolute nightmare to be around. And then, eventually, I have to spend all this time apologizing to my wife for biting her head off just because she asked if I wanted a sandwich while I was trying to rewrite our entire backend infrastructure. It's just... it's a lot. But yeah, when I'm in it, that unstoppable feeling is definitely there for weeks at a time.
Have you ever had a period where you didn't need much sleep, yet you still had a lot of energy?

Oh man, the sleep thing. Yeah. That is... that is probably the most measurable metric of the whole experience, honestly. Because usually, you know, if a normal person gets a bad night of sleep, their cognitive function drops, right? Their latency goes up, they get sluggish, they make errors. But when I'm in one of those zones we were just talking about? It's like my system completely bypasses the need to recharge. 

I will go on these long runs where I am logging maybe... three hours of sleep a night? Max. I'll finally force myself to shut down the monitors and hit the pillow at midnight, but then, without fail, my eyes just snap open sharp at 3 or 4 a.m. And I don't mean I wake up groggy, or I have to drag myself out of bed and stumble to the coffee machine. I mean I wake up completely online. Boot sequence finished, zero lag, hundred percent battery. 

And the weirdest part is, I don't feel tired at all. Not even a little bit. It honestly feels like... like I’ve just been handed this incredible amount of bonus time. Like I found a cheat code for extra hours in the day while the rest of the world is offline. I'll look at the clock, see 3:15 AM, and instead of dreading it or trying to force myself back to sleep, I'm thrilled. I think, great, nobody is going to ping me on Slack for the next five hours. I can dive straight into the code, I can restructure the entire database schema without a single interruption. 

My wife just does not understand it. She'll wake up at 7 a.m. to get ready for her day, and she'll come out to the home office and see I'm already on my third deployment of the morning. She'll ask if I slept at all, and I'll say, yeah, I got three hours, I'm good to go! And she just looks at me like I'm an alien, because who functions on three hours? But if anything, I feel more energized than if I had slept a full eight hours. It’s like sleep just becomes this completely unnecessary legacy process that my brain figured out how to optimize out of the system. It's incredibly efficient, but yeah, it definitely freaks people out when they realize I've been awake since 3 a.m. just burning through tasks like it's nothing.
Have you ever had a period where you felt abnormally happy or euphoric and your friends or family thought you were acting strangely or being overly confident?

Oh, wow, "overly confident" is... well, that's definitely the phrase my wife uses. And my director at work, for that matter. They think I'm being arrogant or, I don't know, totally megalomaniacal when I get into that state. But from my perspective, in that moment, it's not arrogance at all. It's just absolute, undeniable clarity. 

It's like the matrix just decodes itself in front of my eyes, you know? I'll look at the systems we're running, the legacy code, the network topology, and at my worst I honestly believe I’m the only person who can see the whole architecture clearly. I mean, I look around at these other developers and project managers, and it's like they're staring at a single line of code with blinders on, while I'm seeing the entire ecosystem. The front end, the back end, the server load, the future scaling issues... all of it, all at once. 

And because I can see it all so perfectly, I get this overwhelming conviction that we are heading for a catastrophic crash. Like, a total system collapse that nobody else is predicting because their models are just too narrow. And I just know, with absolute, one-hundred-percent certainty, that if people would just follow my plan, I could save the company from a major failure. 

So I start acting on it, right? Because how could I not? I'll start sending these massive, multi-page emails to the VP of Engineering at 2 AM, outlining exactly how we need to rip out the entire backend and rebuild it my way, immediately. I'll take over conference rooms at the office that I haven't even booked, just frantically drawing these incredibly complex diagrams on the whiteboards, mapping out the disaster I'm trying to avert and the exact architecture we need to migrate to. 

And yeah, that's when my wife starts looking at me with that really specific, worried expression. She'll tell me I'm acting strange, that I'm talking way too fast, that I'm being completely unrealistic about my actual role in the company. She'll try to ground me, you know, remind me that I'm a mid-level manager, not the CEO or the CTO. But in my head, during those weeks, titles don't matter at all. The whole ship is sinking and I'm the only one holding the blueprints to the lifeboats! So they see it as this bizarre, inflated ego trip, this massive overconfidence, but to me... I just feel like a prophet trying to warn a village about a flood. I just get so incredibly frustrated that they can't see what is so blindingly obvious to me. But yeah, to answer your question, they definitely notice, and they definitely think I'm acting out of my mind with how confident I get.
Have you ever had a period where you felt abnormally happy or euphoric that lasted for at least one week?

Well, yeah, exactly like I was saying earlier when you asked about the two-week stretches. If I've had it last for two or three weeks, I've definitely had it hit that one-week mark. It always starts out that way. 

Those weeks... I mean, like I mentioned before, some weeks I feel almost electric and completely unstoppable. The first few days of that week are usually pure magic. I'm riding this massive wave of just pure, unadulterated euphoria, feeling like my brain is finally unlocked. Every line of code is flawless, every server deployment goes off without a hitch, and I'm just soaring. 

But even within just a seven-day period, that sharp edge always shows up. It's like the system gets too hot, you know? Overclocked. So I'll be in the middle of this amazing, unstoppable week, feeling completely on top of the world, and then... just the tiniest, most insignificant delay happens. Like my wife just popping her head into the office to ask if I took the dog out, or if I want a glass of water. A totally innocent, normal question! But in that state, my brain doesn't register it as a question. It registers it as a direct threat to my momentum. 

I just snap. I go from this euphoric, on-top-of-the-world feeling to pure, blinding irritation in a fraction of a second. Because in that moment, it honestly feels like everyone around me is colluding to slow me down on purpose. I think I got distracted by trying to optimize the security protocols on my home network router right in the middle of writing it, and then I just forgot about the email entirely. So, technically, no, I didn't quit. And they didn't fire me, thank God. They just gave me that forced time off. I've been at the company for eight years, so I think they know my baseline value when I'm not... you know, redlining like that.

And as for my marriage, no, I would never end it. I mean, I know I put her through absolute hell, like I was saying before. The arguments are exhausting, and I get so unbelievably stubborn and righteous. There was this one night during that same week where we were arguing about the credit card bill for those server racks, and I got so worked up I actually packed a bag. I put my work laptop, three different mechanical keyboards, a soldering iron, and a massive bundle of ethernet cables into a duffel bag and told her I was going to go live in a hotel where I could actually get some work done without being constantly micromanaged. 

But I never made it out the door. I ended up sitting on the floor in the hallway trying to untangle and color-code a CAT6 cable for like three hours until I just kind of ran out of steam. So, the relationship definitely gets strained to the absolute limit, and it takes a lot of apologies and repair work afterward, but I've never actually ended it. She's still here, and I'm still at my job. So, no, I haven't done anything with those kinds of final, permanent consequences. It gets close, but... no.

Yeah, I know we've kind of been circling this, and I talked about the arguments and the project boards, but... if you want to know exactly what that mood actually feels like on the inside during those weeks, it’s... well, it’s complicated. But the problem is, it doesn't just stay as this happy, productive high. Because I'm operating on this entirely different frequency, the rest of the world feels like it's moving through molasses. And that... that is where it gets really ugly. If there is even a tiny delay—like, if a database query takes five seconds too long to load, or if I'm in the middle of a thought and my wife just asks a totally normal, innocent question, like, "Hey, did you remember to take the trash out?" or "Can you look at me for a second?"—I just snap. I go from zero to absolute fury in a millisecond. 

It’s not just normal annoyance, either. It’s this intense, burning frustration, because in that state, I honestly feel like everyone is trying to slow me down on purpose. Like they can see I'm on the verge of this massive breakthrough, this huge architectural leap, and they are actively choosing to drag me back down to their level with these mundane interruptions. I’ll just lash out, completely viciously, because how dare they interrupt the flow, you know? So it’s this really volatile mix. I’m electric, I’m on top of the world, but the second the real world bumps into me... boom. It’s like dropping a wrench across a live circuit board. Everything just sparks and catches fire, and I end up screaming about efficiency to my poor wife who just wanted to know if I wanted a sandwich. So, yeah, the euphoria is there, absolutely, but it’s so brittle. It just shatters into this massive irritability over absolutely nothing.
